name: Canela-Krahô
confidence_why: 4 independent first-hand sources agree (3 agree, 0 refine), none contradicts
catalog_quote: Syllable patterns are as follows: V, VC, CW [=CVV], CVC, CCV, CCW, CCVC. Stress falls on the final syllable of nouns and verbs (and most other words) in isolation.
sweep_summary: Two works with stress in the title, both genuinely about word stress in varieties of cane1242 and both unobtainable in text: Castro Alves 2007 (Apãniekrá chapter, print-only UnB/FINATEC volume; her held 2004 thesis p.44 gives the likely same root-final rule) and Sá 2001/2003 (3-page ABRALIN note on Pykobjê; only the the Internet Archive table of contents survives, the PDF is not archived). Following the Sá lead, I downloaded the open copy of Amado (= Sá) 2004, the USP doctoral thesis on Gavião-Pykobjê, which states predictable final stress (97/93/100% of di-/tri-/polysyllables), weight-insensitive, with stress shifting to the final syllable in compounds — confirming the catalog's fixed: final syllable coding for the Pykobjê dialect; it does not supersede Popjes & Popjes 1986 as the deciding source for Canela-Krahô. Bastos 2006 (acoustic study of Krahô stress) located as a record only. teses.usp.br, sw.npd.ufc.br, Google Scholar and HathiTrust unreachable.

new_statements.quote: O acento da língua é previsível. Do corpus analisado durante o mestrado, cerca de 97% dos dissílabos apresentam a última sílaba acentuada, ou seja, possuem pé dominante à direita. Em relação aos trissílabos, isso ocorre em cerca de 93% e nos polissílabos em 100% dos casos. [...] pode-se classificar o Pykobjê, segundo Hayes (1995), como uma língua que apresenta pé métrico iâmbico moraico, contudo não é sensível ao peso silábico, já que grande parte dos dissílabos apresenta sílaba pesada à esquerda (VC, CVC ou CV:) e sílaba leve à direita
new_statements.translation: Stress in the language is predictable. In the corpus analysed for the MA, about 97% of disyllables have the final syllable stressed, i.e. a right-dominant foot; for trisyllables this holds in about 93% of cases and for polysyllables in 100%. [...] Pykobjê can be classified, following Hayes (1995), as a language with a moraic iambic foot, yet it is not sensitive to syllable weight, since most disyllables have a heavy syllable on the left (VC, CVC or CV:) and a light one on the right.
new_statements.citation: Amado, Rosane de Sá. 2004. Aspectos morfofonológicos do Gavião-Pykobjê. Tese de Doutorado, FFLCH-USP, 183 pp. DOI 10.11606/t.8.2004.tde-22122022-152709
new_statements.reading: Corpus-quantified statement of predictable word-final, weight-insensitive stress for the Pykobjê (Gavião) dialect of cane1242, with the compound rule (p.132) that stress moves to the final syllable of the new word; a small residue of long-vowel words stressed non-finally is treated as lexicalised compounds. Agrees with the catalog's 'fixed-strict final' coding and with the held Popjes & Popjes (Canela) and Castro Alves 2004 (Apãniekrá, root-final) statements.

new_statements.quote: O presente trabalho trata das conexões entre o acento fonológico e o acento fonético em Krahô. [...] Sabendo que em Krahô o acento, com raras exceções, é final, fizemos medições fonéticas com o intuito de verificar se alguma variável fonética caracteriza o acento fonológico. Na primeira parte do trabalho apresentamos o resultado preliminar dessas medições. Nossos próprios resultados levantaram uma série de problemas, dos quais tratamos e tentamos explicar na segunda parte do trabalho, para enfim apresentar, no anexo, nossas medições finais.
new_statements.translation: The present work deals with the connections between phonological stress and phonetic stress in Krahô. [...] Knowing that in Krahô stress, with rare exceptions, is final, we made phonetic measurements with the aim of verifying whether some phonetic variable characterises phonological stress. In the first part of the work we present the preliminary result of these measurements. Our own results raised a series of problems, which we treat and try to explain in the second part of the work, finally presenting, in the appendix, our final measurements.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's fixed: final syllable coding (StressTyp2: final stress) and with the existing Amado 2004 statement for Pykobjê (final, weight-insensitive, ~93-100% of the corpus). Bastos describes the Krahô variety specifically; the 'rare exceptions' echo Amado's small residue of non-finally stressed long-vowel words. Nothing in the abstract contradicts the catalog. Access: the DOI resolves to teses.usp.br, which times out by automated download (also on the two earlier passes); the etnolinguistica.org file link http://www.fflch.usp.br/dl/pos/teses/TIBIRICAleandro.pdf returns 404 live and in every Internet Archive copy (2020-2024, CDX checked); the the Internet Archive availability…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Krahô falls on the final syllable, with rare exceptions (taken as the premise of an instrumental study of the acoustic correlates of that stress). Which syllables count as the exceptions, and whether the study found a reliable phonetic correlate, cannot be read from the abstract.
new_statements.exceptions: 'com raras exceções' (with rare exceptions) — the exceptions are not specified in the abstract.
new_statements.identity_note: Bastos 2006 describes the Krahô variety (Krahô reserve between Itacajá and Goiatins, Tocantins state), one of the Timbira varieties grouped under cane1242 (Central-Southern Timbira); the existing Amado 2004 statement is for the Pykobjê (Gavião) variety of the same glottocode. Both report final stress.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding sentence is verbatim at Popjes & Popjes 1986:190 in the held archive.org scanned (only the '[=CVV]' gloss is editorial). (2) The deciding source is the standard HAL grammar sketch by the long-term SIL fieldworkers;5 and p.16 and whose stress-marked transcriptions show final stress independent of pretonic vowel length — confirms 'fixed final, weight-blind, no secondary described'. The held Castro Alves 2004 PhD (Apãniekrá Canela) refines rather than contradicts: stress is on the last syllable of the ROOT for all word classes, and post-root class-term/diminutive/augmentative syllables (-re, -ti, -rã) are unstressed in her data (kaˈputi, ˈkrure), whereas Popjes 1971 stresses -ti ([plï·ˈti]). Because inflection is entirely prefixal/particulate

sources.note: Pykobjê variety: predictable word-final stress (97% of disyllables, 93% of trisyllables, 100% of polysyllables in the corpus), weight-insensitive, stress shifts to the final syllable in compounds/derivations; a residue (~15% of 29 long-vowel words, p.134) stresses the lengthened non-final syllable, treated as lexical/compound cases. Confirms 'fixed final' for the Pykobjê dialect, adding that final stress overrides syllable weight.

sources.quote: No rule of stress placement stated. 'Com respeito à posição que ocupam em sílabas acentuadas, todos os segmentos vocálicos podem ser núcleos de sílabas tônicas' and oral vowels 'ocorrem também na posição átona pretônica'; 'Esses aspectos serão explorados em pesquisas futuras que considere fatores de natureza rítmica e prosódica'. The tonic/pretonic framing of disyllables is consistent with final stress but is not a statement of it.

It concerns Pykobjê (Gavião do Maranhão), a Glottolog 5.1 dialect of cane1242, so it IS about this languoid though not the Canela/Krahô varieties the catalog's Popjes source describes.
